definition: Overview of hydroelectric power generation and its operational constraints.
core_idea: Hydroelectric dams use flowing water directly to spin a turbine (no steam involved), trapping a river behind a dam to form a lake; the fall of water from lake level down to the river below drives the turbine, and in some cases operators cannot fully halt water flow without risking flooding downstream communities.
key_points: Hydroelectric generation drives a turbine directly with flowing water rather than using steam
Dams typically trap river water to form a lake, with the river located several hundred feet below the lake level
Falling water through the dam spins a water-based turbine to generate electricity
Depending on river flow and lake capacity, operators may not be able to stop water flow without flooding nearby communities
relationships: Power generation technologies: fossil fuel plants
trading_implications: Operational flow constraints mean hydro output cannot always be freely dispatched down, which affects supply flexibility
